1.pericope_label: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem, and besieged it. And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God: which he carried into the land of Shinar to the house of his god; and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch anchor the opening clause in the historical books, where the same event appears as the king becoming a servant and as his being bound, and press the idiom behind the word rendered part, which contracts an expression meaning from end to end, so that what was found throughout contributed its share and much of the whole was taken, the word by itself never meaning a part; on the prophet's name they give the sense God is my judge or God is judging rather than judge of God, note that two other men in the older books bore it, and are more cautious than Clarke about the descent, leaving open whether he came of the royal seed or only of a distinguished family. Ellicott splits the chronological question in two and answers the second in the negative, since the verse does not say the city was taken that year at all: the verb means went rather than came and is the natural word for a Hebrew writing from Babylon, so what is dated is the setting out, the victory at the river falling in the fourth year and the advance on the city only after it; he reads the phrase about the vessels as from one point to another and infers that they went not all at once but on separate occasions, and identifies the god by his fuller compound name, tracing him to an older people and reporting that the second element means one who measures the path of the sun.

Gill keeps two captivities in view, the first leaving the king on his throne as a tributary with Daniel and his companions held as hostages; Calvin dismisses two escapes from the chronological difficulty as frivolous or forced, the one counting the years from the beginning of the reign and the one reckoning from the conquest, and conjectures that either an earlier king of the name is meant or the son's reign is dated while his father still lived; he also refuses to let the doubled sentence about the vessels stand for two events, since it is one statement made twice in different words, the term house standing in that language for any place at all.

Clarke explains what was left behind and why, since the richest pieces went for the service of the foreign god while the rest stayed because the conqueror meant no alteration of the country's constitution, civil or religious, and merely laid it under tribute; he counts three separate removals of the sacred vessels across the years, names the tutelary god of the city, and opens with the man rather than the date, making him of the royal house, carried off very young and bred so thoroughly in the law that he kept it in a heathen court while a slave, with a reputation that became proverbial in his own lifetime; Wesley notes that such divine names were worked into the names of their kings, and that this expedition is where the captives came from, Daniel among them.

Henry gives the outcome and stands back from it: the city was soon mastered, the king seized, the throne left occupied on tribute for eight years until a rebellion ruined it, and from this first deportation most reckon the seventy years, though the destruction came two decades later. What strikes him is one man's life against an empire's, since Daniel was carried off that first year and outlasted the whole seventy, so that one prophet saw the rise, reign and ruin of the monarchy within his own time — such short-lived things are the kingdoms of the earth, and the righteous who watch them take root will see them fall.

debates.question: How can the invasion be dated to the third year of a king who had not yet begun to reign?

positions.position: The verse dates the setting out, not the capture: the verb means went, the natural word for a writer in Babylon, and the rest of the sequence follows from the histories.
Either an earlier king of the same name is meant, or the son's reign is being dated while his father still lived; the usual escapes are frivolous or forced.
There were two captivities in that reign, the first leaving the king tributary and taking hostages.

debates.question: Was Daniel of the royal seed?

positions.position: He was of the royal house, and carried off very young.
It must be left open whether he came of the royal seed or only of one of the most distinguished families.

outliers.claim: Measures one man's life against an empire's, since Daniel outlasted the whole seventy years and so saw the rise, reign and ruin of the monarchy that deported him within his own lifetime.
Explains why the vessels were only partly taken, since the conqueror intended no change to the country's constitution and left what the public worship required.

themes: In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem, and besieged it.

And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God: which he carried into the land of Shinar to the house of his god; and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god.

3.pericope_label: And the king spake unto Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring certain of the children of Israel, and of the king’s seed, and of the princes; Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king’s palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans. And the king appointed them a daily provision of the king’s meat, and of the wine which he drank: so nourishing them three years, that at the end thereof they might stand before the king. Now among these were of the children of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah: Unto whom the prince of the eunuchs gave names: for he gave unto Daniel the name of Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, of Shadrach; and to Mishael, of Meshach; and to Azariah, of Abed–nego.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch say flatly that no satisfactory explanation of the court officer's name has yet been found and identify him as chief marshal of the court, take the first term in the list of qualifications for aptitude rather than attainment, an ability to apply themselves to Chaldean learning, and compare two kings of Judah renamed by their overlords; Ellicott reports the tradition connecting the four youths with the last king of Judah and thinks the context admits it, reasons from the elaborateness of Babylonian science that the training must have begun early and that the king's later astonishment at Daniel's precocity suggests he was young, credits the king with insight enough to prescribe both subjects and length of course, and notices that in one of the new names two letters appear to have been deliberately swapped so that the bearer should not carry a heathen name exactly as it stood.

Gill reports two derivations of the officer's name, one making it a man of angry countenance and the other a man excelling in wit, will not have the youths reckoned children at all but fifteen or twenty on the ground that a few years later Daniel held posts of real eminence, grants the munificence of the royal table while seeing in it a bait laid to make the young men love their new condition and forget the old, and gives the motives for the renaming in ascending order, to make them acceptable, to mark them as naturalised subjects, to make them forget the names their fathers gave, and most of all the God whose name those names carried; Calvin puts the youths at seven or eight, sets out the king's political calculation that boys nourished in his palace would grow estranged from their own people while their noble parentage kept the nation quiet, insists on reading one participle actively since otherwise the repetition would be cold and valueless and finds eloquence intended, and holds that where there is cunning in the world it reigns especially in palaces, so that a king dealing with an obstinate people set out to soften them with luxuries and his feeding of these exiles is not to be reckoned a virtuous action.

Clarke says the title signifies officers about the palace whether the men were literally eunuchs or not, settles for youths and holds the word should be so rendered throughout the book, calls the renaming a mark of dominion and the customary imposition of new names on slaves while working through the etymologies, and turns the three-year course into a complaint against his own age, since three years sufficed here for a language and its sciences where Europe spends seven years at school and as many at university to produce a little Latin, Greek and mathematics and sends out men entitled rather than qualified to teach; Wesley sees an older prophecy fulfilled in the taking of the noble youths, and calls the renaming an act of the king's sovereignty.

debates.question: How old were the youths taken for training?

positions.position: Not children at all but fifteen or twenty, since Daniel held posts of real eminence a few years later.
Seven or eight.
Young, on the evidence of how elaborate the training was and of the king's later astonishment at Daniel's precocity.
Youths rather than children; the word should be rendered so throughout the book.

debates.question: Why were noble youths taken and fed from the king's table?

positions.position: A political calculation: to display the conquest, to hold hostages, to raise servants estranged from their own people, and to keep the nation quiet through fear for its children.
As a bait to make them love their new condition and forget the old.
Because the king had insight enough to prescribe both the subjects and the length of their course.

outliers.claim: Turns the three-year curriculum into an attack on European education, which spends seven years at school and as many at university to produce a little Latin and Greek and men entitled rather than qualified to teach.
Notices that in one of the four new names two letters appear to have been deliberately transposed, so that the bearer should not have to carry a heathen divine name exactly as it stood.

8.pericope_label: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs. And the prince of the eunuchs said unto Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who hath appointed your meat and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse liking than the children which are of your sort? then shall ye make me endanger my head to the king. Then said Daniel to Melzar, whom the prince of the eunuchs had set over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch locate the officer's favour in what he did not do, since he neither dismissed the request as impertinent nor treated it as punishable but respected the conviction behind it and raised only the danger, give the grammar of his answer its force so that the question means he must not see it and the closing phrase means to forfeit one's head, and note the article before the second officer's title, making it a description from words for wine and head, an overseer of the drink; Ellicott says Daniel was cautious from the first for fear of eating what had been consecrated to idols, observes that the diet adopted is the plain one his ancestors kept before entering the land and that the reason it was dropped later stands in the book itself, where at the Persian court an older man changes his rule as age tells, lays the story beside Joseph's at four points, glosses the comparison as the young men's contemporaries, calls the second officer a cellarman rather than a name, and takes the ten days for a round number.

Gill takes the singular verb to mean Daniel first thought of the refusal and moved it to the others, reads the officer's answer as hesitation rather than denial with the man divided between affection and fear, holds that the natural gifts might have ingratiated him but that nothing would have overcome a religious prejudice unless the Lord had worked on the man's heart, takes the second officer's title for a personal name meaning one in full splendour, and thinks ten days long enough for any ill effect to show; Calvin raises the objection to the whole refusal himself, that to the pure all things are pure, that nothing of the kind is recorded of Joseph and that Daniel very likely ate freely later, so abstaining now looks superstitious or morose and if right should have been kept up, answering that the abstinence was a defence against being tampered with rather than a rule about food, praises the officer for what he kept quiet rather than what he granted since the request would have been fatal had it reached the king, and makes the descent to a lower official the mark of a rooted piety that tries every way and does not treat the road as closed.

Clarke gives three grounds for the refusal, unclean animals, animals not properly killed, and animals offered to the gods first, citing a Greek writer who calls the meats at those royal tables victims, has the second officer an officer under the chamberlain with charge of their food, identifies the pulse as seeds and grain, and insists the result was not the diet's doing but a blessing on a diet chosen for religion's sake; Wesley adds that such fare would gratify the flesh and ill suited the exiles' afflicted condition, and calls the refusal a rare pattern of avoiding the occasions of evil.

Henry makes the point that carries the chapter, that they changed Daniel's name but not his nature and that he worked at the books as hard as anyone while drawing the line at the table; on the favour he allows that Daniel deserved it and recommended himself by his temper, but notes that the text says God brought him into favour, since not everyone meets acceptance according to his merits, and what interest we think we have made for ourselves must be acknowledged a gift.

debates.question: Why would the king's food have defiled them?

positions.position: Three grounds: unclean animals, animals not properly killed, and animals offered to the gods before being served.
Those grounds and two more, that such fare would gratify the flesh and ill suited the afflicted condition of the exiles.
Not a rule about food at all, since to the pure all things are pure and Daniel very likely ate freely later; the abstinence was a defence against being tampered with.
Caution from the first, for fear of eating what had been consecrated to idols.

debates.question: Who is to be credited with the officer's compliance?

positions.position: God, since not everyone meets acceptance according to his merits and the interest we think we have made for ourselves must be acknowledged a gift.
God again, since natural gifts would never have overcome a religious prejudice unless the Lord had worked on the man's heart.
The officer himself, in what he refrained from doing: he neither dismissed the request nor treated it as punishable, but respected the conviction and raised only the danger.

outliers.claim: Supplies without meaning to the answer to Calvin's puzzle about why the abstinence was not lifelong, by pointing to the later passage where an older Daniel at the Persian court changes his rule of life as age tells on him.

Reads the descent to a subordinate officer as the test of piety, since after one repulse it would have seemed excusable to stop, and the rooted believer tries every way rather than treating the road as closed.

themes: But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.
Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs.

And the prince of the eunuchs said unto Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who hath appointed your meat and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse liking than the children which are of your sort? then shall ye make me endanger my head to the king.
Then said Daniel to Melzar, whom the prince of the eunuchs had set over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,
Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.

13.pericope_label: Then let our countenances be looked upon before thee, and the countenance of the children that eat of the portion of the king’s meat: and as thou seest, deal with thy servants. So he consented to them in this matter, and proved them ten days. And at the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king’s meat. Thus Melzar took away the portion of their meat, and the wine that they should drink; and gave them pulse. As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams. Now at the end of the days that the king had said he should bring them in, then the prince of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar. And the king communed with them; and among them all was found none like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah: therefore stood they before the king. And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm. And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch have the four brought in at the end of the three years, found more intelligent than all the others educated with them and beyond that superior to every wise man in the kingdom, and on the closing verse make the preposition mark a terminus without any claim about what came after; Ellicott sees God beginning to assert himself among the Babylonians and insists the change of appearance came of free grace and not of the king's meat, divides the two terms for the youths' attainment by giving secular literature to the first and philosophy, theology and perhaps the reading of portents to the second, and guards the closing verse against misreading, since the word means Daniel lived until that year rather than that he prophesied only until then or died in it, the year being named as that of the deliverance.

Gill notes the healthier colour and solid flesh rather than the puffiness of disease, observes what became of the rejected portions, since the steward took them home and four young gentlemen's rations from the royal table over three years made a handsome addition to his income, so that in serving the Lord's people he served himself, rules out the wrong kind of knowledge because men who scrupled at the king's table would not have studied the magic and judicial astrology the Chaldeans were addicted to, and infers from the questioning that the king was himself a man of learning and judgment; Calvin turns the outcome into doctrine, that there is no necessary virtue in bread, which has no life in it and cannot give what it lacks, so that what sustains us is a secret blessing and God has merely breathed the power into the food, makes the steward's compliance an argument about providence rather than kindness, denies that the gift of learning was a reward for frugal living since God's intention was to establish Daniel's authority, and takes the closing verse to mean that Daniel flourished and was acknowledged a prophet through the whole Babylonian period, to the night the last king was killed.

Clarke supplies a test for distinguishing divine dreams, since ordinary dreams signify only as much as they cohere, being products of the body, the mind or the day's circumstances, while one may be reckoned supernatural when nothing in it is preposterous or monstrous and the order holds from beginning to end; Wesley draws the moral that plain fare under a blessing often yields more health than costly fare does to those who eat the fat, agrees that the king's questioning shows his ability and judgment since otherwise he could not have discerned their fitness, and adds that God was pouring contempt on the pride of the Chaldeans and putting honour on the low estate of his own people.

Henry allows that the four were sober and diligent and that their tutors took pains, but ascribes the achievement to God only, and reads the learning both as a balance for what captivity had cost them and as a recompence for their integrity.

debates.question: Was the gift of learning a reward for their abstinence?

positions.position: Yes, in part: it was both a balance for what their captivity had cost them and a recompence for their integrity.
No: it would be wrong to call it a reward for living frugally, since God's intention was to establish Daniel's authority for the prophetic office.
Whatever its ground, it was not of their own sagacity or their teachers' ability, and it was not the forbidden Chaldean arts.

debates.question: What does it mean that Daniel continued to the first year of Cyrus?

positions.position: That he lived until that year, which is named as the year of the deliverance; it does not mean he prophesied only until then or died in it.
The preposition marks a terminus in a wide sense, with no claim at all about what came after.
That he flourished and was acknowledged a prophet through the whole Babylonian period, down to the night the last king of Babylon was killed.

outliers.claim: Turns the outcome of the ten days into a doctrine of nourishment, that bread has no life in it and so cannot give life, and that what feeds the body is a secret blessing which God has breathed into the food.
Offers a working test for telling a divine dream from an ordinary one, that the order and consequence hold unbroken from beginning to end and nothing in it is preposterous or monstrous.
